author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Empty Chair Is Not a Threat
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The chair beside the window had been empty for twelve days.

I knew because Mara had asked whether the teahouse needed another delivery of bread, and Iroh had said, "Only if Mr. Halen returns." He said it lightly, but I noticed his eyes move toward the small table where the old man usually sat.

Halen was not an especially cheerful customer. He came three mornings a week, drank one cup of the house blend, complained about the weather, and left two coins on the table even when the price was lower. He had once informed me that my sweeping technique lacked discipline.

I liked him.

When he stopped coming, I assumed he had found another shop.

Iroh did not.

"Would you like to check on him?" I asked.

"I would," he said. "But I do not wish to make his absence into an accusation."

"Then we can ask whether he's well. He can tell us to go away."

Iroh considered that.

"An excellent outcome, if he is well enough to do so."

We found the address through the delivery notes Halen had voluntarily given the teahouse for winter weather. Iroh checked that the contact permission included welfare visits, not just tea delivery. It did.

He wrapped a small packet of bread and tea leaves, and we walked up Jasmine Steps toward the narrow houses behind the herb gardens.

The path was damp. Water ran through the channels between the stones, carrying the faint smell of rosemary. At Halen's gate, a blue flowerpot lay on its side.

Iroh knocked.

Nothing happened.

He knocked again, then stepped back.

A window opened above us.

"Go away," Halen called.

I looked at Iroh.

He smiled.

"Good morning, Mr. Halen. We noticed you have not visited. We wished to know whether you are well."

"I'm alive."

"An encouraging beginning."

"I don't want tea."

"Then we shall not insist."

The window began to close.

I spoke before I could stop myself.

"Do you need help with the flowerpot?"

There was a pause.

"What?"

"The one by the gate. It's fallen over."

Halen looked down.

"Blasted wind."

"Would you like me to set it upright?"

He considered.

"Yes. Don't break it."

I picked up the pot and found a crack along the base. The soil had spilled into the path, and the plant's roots were exposed.

"This needs a new pot," I said.

Halen sighed.

"Of course it does."

Iroh looked up at him.

"May we come in with it?"

A long silence followed.

Then we heard the stairs.

Halen opened the door wearing a coat over his nightclothes. His hair was uncombed. The house behind him smelled of dust and old paper.

"Five minutes," he said.

We went inside.

The room was filled with boxes. On the table lay a bundle of letters tied with blue string. Halen noticed me looking and put a hand over them.

"Private."

"Of course," I said.

I turned away.

We found a spare pot in the kitchen and moved the plant into it. Iroh made tea only after Halen asked for some. The bread stayed wrapped on the counter until he decided whether he wanted it.

For the first ten minutes we talked about weather and soil.

Then Halen sat down.

"My sister died," he said.

I felt the words more than heard them.

Iroh placed his cup on the table.

"I am sorry."

Halen nodded.

"She used to write to me every week. We argued about everything. The proper way to prune roses. Whether the sea-glass orchard was a waste of good stone. Whether I should stop eating so much bread."

I looked at the bundle of letters.

He followed my glance.

"I don't want anyone to read them."

"Then nobody will," I said.

Halen stared at the table.

"I stopped coming to the teahouse because she liked it. She always asked whether I had seen the old general who served jasmine tea. I would tell her he was overbearing."

Iroh smiled faintly.

"An accurate assessment."

Halen's mouth twitched.

"I didn't want to sit in the chair and think about how I couldn't tell her it was raining."

I understood then why the empty chair mattered. Not because a regular customer had stopped spending coins, but because a small ordinary place had become painful to enter.

"Do you want us to keep the chair for you?" I asked.

Halen looked startled.

"No."

"All right."

He frowned.

"You're not going to insist?"

"No. You can come back if you want. You can choose a different seat. Or you can stay home."

Iroh nodded.

"The table will remain part of the teahouse, but you are not a duty it must fulfill."

Halen looked at him for a long moment.

"You're a strange man."

"Often."

He finally unwrapped the bread.

We left after half an hour, not because we were unwelcome but because Halen had asked for some quiet. He kept the plant on the windowsill and accepted the tea leaves.

On the walk back, Iroh was silent.

"Are you thinking about Lu Ten?" I asked.

He nodded.

"Yes."

I took his hand.

"Would you like to talk?"

"Not today."

"All right."

He looked grateful for the simplicity of the answer.

At the teahouse, the chair by the window remained empty. We cleaned it like every other chair and set the day's menu on the table. Iroh did not leave a cup waiting. I did not watch the door every few minutes.

A week later, Halen returned.

He walked in carrying the repaired flowerpot and set it on the counter.

"Your tea was too strong," he told Iroh.

"Then I shall make it weaker."

"And the bread was too sweet."

"Mara will be devastated."

He glanced toward the window seat.

Then he chose a table near the back.

Iroh carried his tea there without comment.

After closing, I found him washing the cups alone. I stood beside him and took a towel.

"Happy?" I asked.

"Relieved."

"That he came back?"

"That he chose to."

I smiled.

Iroh turned toward me, his hands damp from the washbasin.

"Thank you for not making his grief into a project."

"I almost did."

"Yes," he said gently. "So did I."

I leaned close enough to feel his breath against my cheek.

"Do you want company tonight?"

He touched the back of my hand.

"Very much."

The kiss was soft and brief, a promise of nothing more than being together when we both wanted it.

The next morning, the chair by the window was occupied by a new customer who asked whether the house blend contained citrus.

It did.

Halen sat at the back with his tea, reading a letter he had chosen to bring.

Nobody asked who it was from.
